topic: diffusion-network inference; cascades; temporal concept drift
status: bounded research-design lead from one sampled full text; novelty not established
claim: The sampled 2012 method has a submodular guarantee, higher recall than a leading baseline in several low-cascade synthetic regimes, and a large synthetic scale result. Yet the model assumes a fixed network and its real-data reference graph uses hyperlinks as a proxy for information propagation. This leaves a testable question: how quickly does recovery degrade when the underlying graph changes, and can rolling-window or change-point-aware inference improve time-local recovery?
positive_evidence: The paper sums over all propagation trees and uses greedy submodular optimization; on tested synthetic networks it often reaches higher recall than NetInf with few cascades.
The paper reports scalability tests at 100,000 and 200,000 nodes with 10,000 cascades, at 10.12 and 12.14 ms per added edge respectively.
The real-data study is based on 172M+ MemeTracker articles/blog posts, but uses hyperlink cascades among 1,000 selected sites and evaluates against a graph constructed from hyperlinks.
counterevidence: All compared methods assume cascades propagate over a fixed network; real social or information networks can evolve, so the fixed-network premise limits temporal extrapolation.
On synthetic data the gap to NetInf narrows as more cascades are observed, and NetRate outperforms the method for one hierarchical network topology.
Hyperlinks are only a proxy for causal information transmission; the paper itself notes that richer qualitative evidence from textual phrases is beyond scope.

sources.sections: Sections 2 and 4-5; synthetic and MemeTracker results

falsifiable_test: Generate cascades on graphs with controlled edge-addition/deletion rates and compare fixed-network inference to rolling-window and change-point-aware approaches; then use time-sliced real cascade data only where time-local reference edges can be independently established. Report time-local precision/recall, recovery lag after change, transmission-rate calibration, and compute per update. The lead weakens if fixed-network inference remains equally accurate and timely across drift rates; strengthens if temporal adaptation improves held-out recovery at acceptable compute. Not run here.
limitations: One sampled source in one cell. No causal real-world ground truth was found or constructed, algorithms were not run, and temporal inference follow-up literature was not exhaustively reviewed. The question is a hypothesis, not a novelty claim.

topic: differential privacy; adaptive k-way marginal queries; small databases
status: bounded systems-evaluation lead from one sampled full text; novelty not established
claim: The sampled paper proves an important `(ε,δ)`-DP accuracy/runtime tradeoff for adaptively chosen k-way marginals on small databases, including ±0.01 error with probability ≥0.99 under stated database-size conditions. Its per-query runtime remains polynomial in n and subexponential in d, while ε, δ, query count, k, and database size all affect the guarantee. The practical question is whether the theoretical regime yields wall-clock wins over private multiplicative weights or noise baselines at matched privacy and utility on relevant finite workloads.
positive_evidence: Theorem 1.1 handles adaptively selected queries and gives worst-case additive error at most 0.01 on every query with probability at least 0.99 under its explicit sample-size condition.

The paper reports a faster private online mechanism using a new low-weight representation and a polynomial approximation to OR; its lower bound establishes tightness for that polynomial approach in a parameter regime.
The authors discuss private multiplicative weights as practical on some datasets, providing a meaningful systems baseline and clarifying the paper's target as an efficiency/sample-size regime.
counterevidence: Subexponential-in-dimension running time can still be impractical, and the error guarantee requires enough records as a function of dimension, query sequence length, privacy parameters, and k.
The polynomial lower bound is specific to a low-weight polynomial approximation route; it is not an impossibility result for all DP algorithms or representations.

Related algorithms for marginal release already existed (including the paper's cited 2012 work), and the paper itself compares different database-size/runtime regimes; no generic absence-of-methods claim follows.

sources.sections: Theorem 1.1; Corollary 1.2; Sections 4-5 and Future Directions

falsifiable_test: Benchmark the theorem's algorithm, private multiplicative weights, and appropriate noise baselines over d, k, n, ε, δ, and adaptive query count. Report runtime, memory, worst-case/empirical query error, and formal privacy accounting separately. The lead weakens if the proposed mechanism does not improve finite-regime runtime or database-size needs at matched privacy/error; it strengthens if the gains are repeatable across held-out workloads. No implementation or privacy audit was run here.
limitations: One theory paper and its own related-work discussion; no current comprehensive search for later mechanisms, no reimplementation, and no new privacy proof. This is a bounded evaluation question, not a claim that DP marginals remain unsolved.

topic: similarity-preserving hashing; approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval; sparse binary codes
status: bounded benchmark-design lead from one sampled full text; novelty not established
claim: SparseHash reports a real precision/recall improvement on CIFAR-10 and NUS-WIDE, but the same paper shows that its retrieval backend changes the speed conclusion: for 48-bit CIFAR codes, lookup-table search is faster at Hamming radii 0-1, while brute-force search is faster at radius 2. Thus code sparsity and retrieval quality alone do not establish end-to-end search efficiency; the index, radius, candidate count, memory, and similarity-label definition must be included.
positive_evidence: SparseHash uses an ℓ1-regularized ISTA-type encoder and reports higher recall at similar precision than dense codes with comparable degrees of freedom; 128-bit CIFAR codes average about 6% nonzero elements.
The paper reports results across CIFAR-10 and NUS-WIDE plus image-tag retrieval, using mAP, precision/recall, and F1, so the evidence is not limited to one scalar metric.

The authors explicitly compare retrieval timing and observe that sparse codes retrieve partial collisions at low radii with lower computational cost than dense counterparts in their tested implementation.
counterevidence: At Hamming radius 2 on CIFAR-10, brute-force retrieval is faster than lookup-table search; the speed advantage is therefore backend- and operating-point-dependent.
Similarity is defined through shared dataset classes/concepts; high benchmark retrieval scores do not establish open-ended semantic relevance.
CIFAR uses 200 training images per class and NUS-WIDE uses 100,000 training pairs, so the training and label protocol limit generalization claims.

sources.sections: Sections 3-6; CIFAR/NUS evaluation protocol, Figure 3, Tables 5-6 and conclusions

falsifiable_test: Compare SparseHash with dense baselines under matched training labels, code storage, index implementation, and query sets while sweeping code length and Hamming radius. Measure precision/recall/mAP jointly with p50/p95 latency, candidates visited, index memory, and build/update costs. The lead weakens if sparsity cannot improve the quality-latency-memory frontier after backend switching; strengthens if gains persist across held-out datasets and similarity definitions. Not run here.
limitations: One sampled source and two benchmark families; no reimplementation, current dataset suite, or comprehensive search for successors. This is an evaluation design, not a novelty claim.
